title: Let the family’s traditions lead the festive menu
focus: Discuss the regional dishes, snacks and sweets that make Diwali meaningful to your guests. A chaat welcome, a seated family meal and a larger office celebration can each have their own structure. Confirm vegetarian, Jain and other observances specifically, including ingredients and preparation requirements. Live stations need suitable space and service time, so review them with the venue before finalising the menu. Coordinate mithai, dessert and drinks with the rest of the meal to create a generous, balanced celebration.

sections.title: Build the celebration around your family’s food traditions
paragraphs: Tell us the dishes that make Diwali feel familiar to your family or team. You may want a fully vegetarian menu, a regional Indian selection or separate vegetarian and non-vegetarian options. Confirm Jain observances and other ingredient exclusions explicitly, as the details vary between households and guests.

A standing party can begin with passed bites before a main meal. A chaat counter adds an interactive element, while a buffet may work better where everyone will eat at a similar time. Discuss the preparation space, power requirements and service area before including a live station in the menu.

Mithai, desserts and drinks should fit the rest of the selection and the length of the gathering. Share the adult and child counts, any allergies and the timings for greetings or other important moments. The final quote should identify the food, service team, equipment, crockery and clear-down agreed for your celebration.

sections.title: Choose a regional direction before expanding the selection
paragraphs: A broad cuisine name can cover many different dishes and traditions. Share the region, flavours or family favourites you have in mind so the chef can build a menu with a clear identity. If there are particular ingredients or preparations you expect, describe them rather than relying only on a familiar dish name.

A focused menu often feels more coherent than a long list of unrelated favourites. Think about how starters, main dishes, sides and desserts complement one another, and how they will be served. The menu should offer enough variety for the group while remaining practical for the kitchen and service format.

Tell us about spice preferences and essential dietary requirements early. These may affect the choice of dishes as well as individual recipes. The final selection can then reflect the food you enjoy with a clear understanding of what will be prepared for your occasion.

sections.title: Make plant-based food a complete experience
paragraphs: A plant-based menu should offer substance, contrast and variety. Consider a combination of vegetables, grains, legumes and sauces, with textures that make the meal satisfying from the first course to the last. The aim is a selection guests will enjoy for its flavour and balance.

Be precise about the brief. Vegetarian, vegan and dairy-free requests are different, and allergies require separate attention. Ingredients in stocks, dressings, breads and desserts should be reviewed as carefully as the main dishes. If some guests are eating another menu, discuss how alternatives will be identified and served.

Choose dishes that suit the occasion. Small handheld bites can work well for a reception, while a seated meal may call for a more substantial centrepiece. A considered plant-based option belongs within the overall menu and service plan, with its own proper portion and presentation.

sections.title: List the equipment before calling the plan complete
paragraphs: Food, kitchen equipment and table items are separate parts of a catering brief. Confirm what the venue supplies and what the catering team needs to bring. Depending on the format, that may include preparation equipment, holding equipment, serving utensils, crockery, glassware or linen.

A photograph of a styled event does not establish what is included in your own package. If you want the same type of table setup or service display, ask for those items to be identified in the proposal. This is particularly useful when the property has limited kitchen facilities or the event uses more than one dining area.

Also agree how equipment will arrive, be set up and be collected. Access restrictions and collection times can affect the plan. A clear equipment list helps the team prepare properly and gives you a practical way to check that the venue is ready before guests arrive.
